video.title: Shoulder Adduction Unlocks the Tennis Forehand

classification.reason: The coach explains how shoulder adduction serves as the final link of the forehand swing and demonstrates how to position the body and contact zone to harness it.

problem.title_as_question: How Does Shoulder Adduction Unlock the Tennis Forehand?
problem.definition: Shoulder adduction is naturally a sideways pulling and turning-over motion. To hit the ball clean and forward toward the target, the player must align their body, elbow, and contact zone so this natural motion drives back to front.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of forehand kinetic chain and contact zone
problem.target_player: 2.5 to 4.5 level players who want to stop missing and hit consistent forehands

symptoms.description: The ball is pulled sideways and down off the racket when shoulder adduction occurs naively.
Racket face turns completely over prematurely through contact, severely closing the string angle.
Shanking or framing the ball when it is positioned too far away or out of the adduction zone.

causes.statement: Natural shoulder adduction is a rotational pulling motion across the body, which travels sideways rather than back to front unless properly aligned.
Shoulder adduction naturally couples with internal shoulder rotation, causing the hand and racket face to turn over prematurely if unmanaged.
The ball is not probed into the correct spatial contact zone relative to the body, leaving the shoulder unable to adduct or already fully adducted.
The hitting elbow is stuck behind the plane of the hips, preventing shoulder adduction from creating a forward swing path.
The hitting shoulder fails to advance in front of the non-hitting shoulder on standard groundstrokes.

angles.summary: Shoulder adduction is the final link in the kinetic chain; the elbow must pass the hip plane and the hitting shoulder must pass the non-hitting shoulder for this link to move back to front.
You do not need full torso uncoiling or explosive leg drive to make clean contact; mastering the final adduction link alone is sufficient to rally consistently.
Players must first internalize the physical feeling of the arm adducting through contact with a stable, consistent string angle before timing moving balls.
Adjusting to low, high, wide, or jammed balls requires tilting the body or altering arm path so that shoulder adduction can still operate through contact.

solutions.summary: Perform comfortable shadow swings through the final arm motion and check that the strings hold a slight downward tilt at contact rather than rolling over.
solutions.external_goal: Check string angle at contact to ensure slight downward tilt

solutions.summary: Ensure the forward swing pulls forward until the elbow clears the hip plane and the hitting shoulder passes the non-hitting shoulder before adducting.
Keep the racket face orientation mostly stable through the contact zone, allowing at most roughly 10 degrees of closure instead of turning over the ball.
solutions.external_goal: Maintain string angle through contact zone with only subtle closure

solutions.summary: Probe low balls by tilting the hips rather than just dropping the arm, keeping the shoulder in the identical adduction corridor for a back-to-front drive.
solutions.external_goal: Tilt hips to align with low ball height

solutions.summary: Once the physical feeling of stable string adduction is ingrained, practice reading incoming balls and positioning yourself so the ball arrives in that exact adduction zone.
solutions.external_goal: Position feet to set the ball into the pre-established adduction window
